You link ideas in a speech or an argumentative text with formal-register connectors: addition, opposition, concession, cause, consequence and structure.
Music is expensive. Now, it brings in more than it costs.
Admittedly, it’s more elegant, but it’s also harder.
Music is not a luxury. Indeed, it has changed these children’s lives.
Lille has one orchestra. Marseille, on the other hand, has two.
It was raining. Consequently, the concert was cancelled.
Add arguments with de plus, en outre, par ailleurs, d’ailleurs, non seulement… mais aussi.
Express opposition and concession with cependant, toutefois, néanmoins, en revanche, certes… mais.
Justify with en effet and car, without confusing “en effet” with “in fact”.
Draw conclusions with donc, ainsi, par conséquent, c’est pourquoi.
Use “or” and structure your speech with d’abord, ensuite, enfin, quant à.

Saturday, 17 January 2032. Inès, 14, is taking part in a national eloquence contest on the topic “Is culture a luxury?”. Her first draft doesn’t work. Claire Vasseur, director of the Conservatoire, helps her improve it.
Mrs Vasseur, I’ve written my speech, but it doesn’t work. All my sentences start with “and” or “but”.
That’s normal. When we speak, that’s how we talk. Now, a speech is written text that is said aloud. You need connectors.
For example. First, you set out the problem. Then you give your arguments. Finally, you conclude. And between the arguments, you build bridges: in addition, furthermore, moreover.
And what if I want to say the opposite of what I’ve just said?
Then you have a choice: however, yet, nevertheless, on the other hand. But careful, they are not identical. “En revanche” compares two things. “Toutefois” limits what you’ve just said.
And “en effet”? My French teacher crossed it out three times in my paper.
Because you use it like “really”. Now, “en effet” is for justifying. You say something, then you explain it: “Music is not a luxury. Indeed, it has changed the lives of seven hundred children.”
Ah. And “or”, precisely? You’ve said it twice.
“Or” is the secret weapon. It introduces a new fact that changes everything. “People say culture is a luxury. Now, at La Duchère, it has brought absenteeism down.” So the starting idea is false.
Admittedly, it’s more elegant. But I’m afraid it sounds… too serious.
(she laughs) You’ve just used “certes… mais”. You see? You already have them. As for the tone, don’t worry: it’s your voice that will give it, not your connectors.
(“par ailleurs” = moreover, on the other hand)
At B2 level (and in the DELF exam), your text is also marked for “cohérence et cohésion”: how you link ideas. “Et” and “aussi” are no longer enough:
De plus, le projet coûte peu.
En outre, il crée des emplois.
Par ailleurs, les parents sont ravis.
Non seulement ils jouent, mais aussi ils composent.
“D’ailleurs” brings extra proof for what you have already said: “Elle parle bien. D’ailleurs, elle a gagné un prix.” “Par ailleurs” opens a new, related topic.
To nuance or contradict, you have several connectors. They are not perfect synonyms:
Le projet est utile. Toutefois, il coûte cher.
Il était fatigué. Néanmoins, il a joué.
Il a travaillé. Pourtant, il a échoué.
Lille a un orchestre. Marseille, en revanche, en a deux.
Certes, c’est cher, mais c’est utile.
“Par contre” is very common in speech, but in careful writing “en revanche” is preferred. In the DELF, write “en revanche”!
“En effet” does NOT mean “really” or “in fact”. It justifies a previous statement, like a “for” placed at the start of the sentence:
Music is not a luxury. Indeed (for), it has changed these children’s lives.
The concert was cancelled, for it was raining.
Since you’re here, help me. (known cause)
“In fact” = “en fait” (with the “t” pronounced), not “en effet”! “En fait, je n’ai pas compris.” = “In fact, I didn’t understand.”
Il pleuvait, donc nous sommes restés.
Ainsi, le réseau a été sauvé.
Par conséquent, le concert est annulé.
C’est pourquoi je vous demande de venir.
Il a parlé fort, si bien que tout le monde a entendu.
Bref, la culture n’est pas un luxe.
In very careful writing, “ainsi” at the start of a sentence can be followed by inversion: “Ainsi faut-il agir vite.” It is not compulsory.
5. “Or” and the structure of a speech
“Or” introduces a new fact that changes the direction of the reasoning. It is typical of argumentation:
People say culture is a luxury. Now, it has brought absenteeism down.
On the one hand… on the other hand…
As for the tone, don’t worry.
“Or” does NOT mean “or” (= “ou”), nor “gold” in this context. Romanian also has a literary “or” with exactly the same meaning: “Or, tocmai asta e problema.”
“Music is not a luxury. ___, it has changed these children’s lives.” (justification)
“Lille has one orchestra. Marseille, ___, has two.” (comparison)
Which connector introduces a new fact that changes the reasoning?
In careful writing, instead of “par contre” you use…
Admittedly, it’s expensive, but it’s useful.
Pourquoi le discours d’Inès ne marche-t-il pas ?
Toutes ses phrases commencent par « et » ou « mais »
Selon Claire, à quoi sert « en effet » ?
Quel connecteur Inès utilise-t-elle sans s’en rendre compte ?
He was tired. Nevertheless, he played the whole concert.
Not only do they play, they also compose.

On 3 January 2032, Henri-Ion turned one. For his birthday, he gave the whole family a present nobody expected: his first steps. He stood up holding on to the sofa, let go of the cushion, and took four steps to his sister. Then he sat down hard on the rug, very proud of himself, looking at everyone as if he had just crossed the Atlantic.

Rose-Hélène clapped, then declared that she had walked much earlier, at ten months. Ioana checked the health record: it wasn’t true, she had walked at fourteen months. Rose-Hélène replied that the record was wrong. She was nearly four, and she had already understood that you can say anything, as long as you say it with confidence.

That same month, Claire Vasseur received a letter from the Ministry of Education. A big national eloquence contest, “Les Voix de demain” (“Tomorrow’s Voices”), was open to middle-school pupils all over France. This year’s topic was printed in large letters at the top of the page: “Is culture a luxury?” Claire read the letter twice. Then she thought of Inès.

Inès was fourteen and in her last year of middle school, at the La Duchère collège. Since the minister’s visit, the whole neighbourhood knew her name. Yet when Claire suggested she take part, she refused at first. “Me, I play the clarinet,” she said. “I don’t talk. Talking is for people who went to university.”

Claire didn’t insist. She just put her phone on the table, with the video of the minister’s visit, the one Théo had discreetly filmed at the back of the hall, and pressed “play”. It showed a teenager with a clarinet walking up to a minister and saying four sentences to him. Four sentences that had helped save twelve orchestras. Inès looked at the screen without saying anything.

“You don’t need to have gone to university,” said Claire. “You need to have something to say. And you have.” Inès asked how long the speech lasted. Five minutes. She asked whether it had to be learnt by heart. Yes. She asked whether there would be many people. A thousand, for the final, in Paris. Inès swallowed hard. Then she said yes.

The first draft was a disaster. Inès brought it to Claire on Saturday 17 January, folded in four in her coat pocket. There were good ideas, a lot of emotion, and every other sentence began with “and” or “but”. Claire read it in silence, a pencil in her hand, without crossing anything out. Then she smiled and said: “Right. We’re going to talk about connectors.”

They worked for three hours that Saturday, in Claire’s office at the Conservatoire. Claire explained to her that a speech is like a house. The ideas are the rooms. The connectors are the doors. Without doors, you stay shut in a single room. With the wrong doors, you get lost. Inès wrote the sentence in her notebook, at the top of a blank page, and underlined it twice.

In the evening, Inès called Théo. She read him a sentence: “Music is expensive. Now, it brings in more than it costs.” Théo said it was very good. To tease him, Inès asked whether he knew what “or” meant. He answered, very seriously, that yes, of course, it was the yellow metal (gold). Inès hung up laughing. She spent the evening explaining “or” to her little sister.

All through January she rewrote her speech. Seven versions. She wrote them in the evening, at the kitchen table, while her mother, a night-shift care assistant, slept a little before leaving for the hospital. Each version was shorter than the one before. Claire had told her that a good speech isn’t when you have nothing left to add. It’s when you have nothing left to take out.

Amina sent her a spreadsheet. Of course. A two-page spreadsheet with the network’s figures since 2028: number of children, rehearsal hours, absenteeism, entries to the Conservatoire, answers to a questionnaire about the future. Inès studied it for an hour. Then she kept a single figure. Just one. When Amina found out, she said that was exactly the right thing to do. Then she opened a new spreadsheet.

Julien, for his part, lent her something more precious. One evening he went up to La Duchère with an envelope. Inside was a photocopy of the letter Odile had left him. Only one sentence was underlined: “Leave your door open.” Julien told Inès she could use it if she wanted. Inès asked whether Odile would have agreed. Julien thought about it. “I think she would have insisted that you use it.”

Meanwhile, Rose-Hélène was preparing a big event too. Mrs Chevalier’s class had learnt Henri’s waltz for the end-of-January school party. Twenty-five children aged three and four, with plastic recorders, tambourines and triangles. Rose-Hélène, of course, played the harmonica. And she was the one who had to whistle during the silence, because nobody else could whistle.

The party took place on Friday 30 January, in the covered playground of the school on rue Dumenge. The result was dreadful and magnificent. The recorders played three different waltzes at the same time. The triangle rang whenever it liked. But at the moment of silence, the twenty-five children stopped together, perfectly, like a single person. And Rose-Hélène whistled.

Under the shelter, the parents fell silent. Some didn’t know the story. Others had seen it in Marc Delorme’s video. A mother in the front row began to cry without knowing why. At the end, Mrs Chevalier took the microphone and simply said: “This silence is for Madame Odile, who lived on rue d’Austerlitz, and who whistled.”

On 7 February, Inès competed in the regional final, at Lyon city hall, in the big function room. There were fifteen middle-school pupils from the whole region. She went ninth, after a boy from Saint-Étienne who had made the whole room laugh. Inès didn’t want to make people laugh. She stepped onto the platform, put her hands on the lectern, and fell silent.

She stayed silent a long time. About eight bars, if you had counted in three-four time. In the room, someone coughed. The chairman of the jury looked up from his notes. Théo, at the back, thought she had forgotten her text. Then Inès began, in a calm voice: “Ladies and gentlemen, this silence is expensive. Indeed, it nearly cost twelve orchestras.”

Nobody told the rest in quite the same way. Théo said she had spoken like a lawyer. Claire said she had spoken like a musician, respecting the strong and weak beats. Her mother, who had taken the night off to come, only said that she had spoken like Inès, and that she hadn’t known her daughter could speak like that.

In the front row of the audience sat a white-haired man taking notes. It was Bernard Delorme. He had come without telling anyone. When the jury announced that Inès had come first and would go to Paris, he was the first to stand up and applaud. Then he came to shake her hand. “Mademoiselle,” he said, “you have convinced me. Now, I am very hard to convince.”

Lucia, meanwhile, was entering her fifth month. On 12 February, the scan showed that the baby was a boy. Radu came out of the hospital shouting in the street, as if he had won a match. Then, in the car, the discussion began. A first name was needed. And in this family, choosing a first name was never simple.

Radu had prepared his arguments like an engineer. “On the one hand,” he said at the table the following Sunday, “we need a name that can be pronounced in Romanian and in French. On the other hand, we need a name that isn’t already taken in the family. Consequently, not Henri, not Ion, not Dan.” Lucia listened to the end without interrupting him. Then she said she had already chosen.

She wouldn’t say which. “However,” she added with a smile, “I can tell you it’s a sailor’s name.” Radu protested that he was the father and had the right to know. Lucia replied that he would find out in May, like everyone else. Rose-Hélène suggested “Harmonica”. The suggestion was noted, but not adopted.

Inès, for her part, was preparing for Paris. Claire had her rehearse her speech three times a week, in the empty Salle Hélène Morel, in front of the armchair covered with the blue shawl. It was Inès’s idea. She said she needed an audience, and that Odile was the best possible audience, because she never interrupted her and never looked at her watch.

The national final took place on Saturday 13 March, at the Odéon theatre in Paris. Twelve finalists from all over France, and even from overseas: a boy from Guadeloupe, a girl from Réunion. The jury was chaired by a great actress. And in the auditorium there were a thousand people, including, in the third row, the Minister of Culture and his daughter.

It was the minister’s daughter who had insisted on coming. Her name was Clémence. She was twelve and played the violin. Since the video, she had learnt Henri’s waltz, and she played it, her father had told Lenoir, “with the silence, always with the silence, even when she plays alone in her room”. She absolutely wanted to meet the girl with the clarinet.

The whole family had made the trip. Julien, Ioana, the two children, Théo, Claire, Amina, Inès’s mother, and even Isabelle, who had come with a little bag of dried lime flowers. Yves Le Goff had come up from Nantes by train. He was carrying a sports bag that made a metallic noise with every step. Nobody dared ask him what was in it.

Inès drew her running order: twelfth. The last. She went pale. Claire told her it was the best place, because the jury always remembers the last one. Inès answered that the jury also remembered the last one when they were bad. Claire admitted that was true. Then she gave her a square of dark chocolate, her personal remedy for stage fright.

The first eleven speeches were excellent. A girl from Strasbourg had spoken about libraries. A boy from Marseille had spoken about rap. And the boy from Guadeloupe, Kylian, had spoken about his grandmother, who sang in Creole while peeling vegetables, and who could neither read nor write. At the end of his speech, half the audience had tears in their eyes.

Then Inès was called. She walked out onto the big stage of the Odéon, under the gilded chandeliers, in her old jacket and trainers. She put her hands on the lectern. And she fell silent. Exactly as in Lyon. A thousand people waited. In the silence, from the third row, a small voice whistled three notes. It was Clémence, the minister’s daughter.

Then, at the back of the hall, another small voice, much more off-key, answered with the next three notes. It was Rose-Hélène. Ioana tried to hush her, but it was too late. In the hall, almost nobody understood what was happening. On stage, Inès smiled. For the first time since the morning, she was no longer afraid.

“Ladies and gentlemen,” she began, “I am asked whether culture is a luxury. Admittedly, it costs money. I don’t deny it. Now, a few months ago, someone wanted to abolish twelve children’s orchestras to save money. And it was children who whistled to save them. You have just heard them.”

Then she spoke about Odile. About an old lady who whistled on the other side of a landing, and who had taught a little girl that you can answer someone who is no longer there. She spoke about Lucien Roux and his clarinet, which she was now holding in her hands. She spoke about a sailor who had lost two fingers and had learnt the harmonica so he could go on playing.

Finally, she gave her one figure. “In my neighbourhood,” she said, “before the orchestra, one child in three didn’t believe they could do anything other than what their parents did. Today, it’s only one in ten. I don’t know how much that costs. I only know it isn’t a luxury. It’s a door. And I’m asking you to leave it open.”

She bowed. There was a second of silence, then the whole audience stood up. In the third row, the minister was applauding on his feet, next to his daughter. At the back, Yves Le Goff was shouting “Bravo, sailor!” in his big Breton voice. The president of the jury had to wait a long time before she could speak.

Inès didn’t win first prize. The jury gave it to Kylian, the boy from Guadeloupe, and she was the first to go and hug him. She received second prize and the audience award, with an ovation that lasted almost two minutes. Later she told Claire she was happy like that. “Besides,” she added, “his grandmother deserved it more than me.”

After the ceremony there was a reception in the theatre foyer. That was where they finally understood what Yves’s sports bag contained. A cast-iron pan. A small camping stove. A litre of galette batter. And a pot of salted butter. Before anyone could stop him, he had lit the stove in the middle of the Odéon foyer.

A security guard came over. Yves looked down at him from his full height, with his cane and his eighty-eight years. “Young man,” he said, “I promised my friends in Lyon I would make your minister taste galettes. Now, a Breton always keeps his promises.” The guard looked at the minister. The minister burst out laughing and signalled to let him carry on.

Minister Desforges ate three galettes. Standing up, with his fingers, like everyone else. Between the second and the third, he took Julien aside. “Mr Moreau,” he said, “I must confess something. When I came to La Duchère, I didn’t believe music could change anything at all. However, my daughter proves me wrong every evening.”

Meanwhile, Clémence and Inès had found each other. They sat in a corner of the foyer, the violinist and the clarinettist, and talked for an hour. About music, school, boys, parents who were too strict. Before leaving, they exchanged numbers. Rose-Hélène, sitting on the floor between them, demanded that hers be noted too. She didn’t have a phone.

On the train home, Inès fell asleep on her mother’s shoulder, the clarinet on her knees, the audience award trophy in her bag. Claire watched her sleep. Julien asked her what she was thinking about. “I think she has many more speeches to give,” Claire replied. “And I doubt anyone can stop her. Fortunately.”

Spring came. Isabelle had chosen a date for the sea: Saturday 10 April. It was the day in 1971 when Odile had passed her third-year medical exam, two months before meeting Henri. Isabelle had discovered it in an old diary of her mother’s, kept in the sea chest with the logbooks.

They went down to Marseille on the Friday evening: Isabelle, Yves, Julien, Ioana and the two children. Mr Benhamou was waiting for them at Saint-Charles station. He had organised everything. His cousin Farid was a fisherman at the Vallon des Auffes, a tiny harbour hidden below the Corniche, and he had agreed to take them out to sea the next morning on his boat.

On Saturday the sea was calm, an almost violet blue. Farid’s boat was called “Belle-Mère” (“Mother-in-law”), which had made Yves laugh for ten minutes. They left the little harbour at eight. Henri-Ion, in his orange life jacket, eyed the water suspiciously. Rose-Hélène held the harmonica box against her heart, like a treasure.

Yves asked Farid to head out to the open sea, opposite the Frioul islands. That was where, he explained, Henri and he used to drop anchor when they came back from a long voyage, before entering the Vieux-Port. You could see the whole city, Notre-Dame-de-la-Garde at the very top, and the ships coming in and going out. Henri used to say it was the most beautiful view in the world.

Farid cut the engine. The boat stopped and began to rock gently. There was nothing left but the sound of the water against the hull and the cries of the gulls. Isabelle took the urn out of her bag. It was a small box of pale wood, very simple. She held it on her knees for a long time without opening it.

Nobody spoke. Then Yves took an old cassette player out of his pocket, the kind of device you only find at flea markets now. He had brought the Dakar cassette. He pressed the button. And in the middle of the sea, opposite Marseille, Henri’s harmonica began to play, with his breath, with his wrong notes, with his voice saying: “Yves, stop that thing of yours.”

Rose-Hélène recognised the waltz at once. She opened the box, took the harmonica of her great-grandfather by heart, and played along with the cassette. Henri in 1978 and Rose-Hélène in 2032, on the same sea, the same waltz. Yves closed his eyes. Ioana took Julien’s hand.

At the third verse, at the moment of silence, Julien stopped the cassette. Rose-Hélène stopped too. Eight bars. Isabelle opened the box and let her mother’s ashes fall into the blue water, gently, slowly, leaning over the side. The wind took them. The sea accepted them. Then Rose-Hélène whistled.

This time, nobody whistled after her. There was no need. Yves restarted the cassette, and the waltz resumed where it had stopped, right to the end. Isabelle threw into the sea the little bag of dried lime flowers she had taken to Paris. The flowers floated for a long time, yellow on blue, before disappearing.

Farid, who didn’t know the story, had taken off his cap. When they got back to the harbour, he refused to be paid. “Where I come from,” he said, “you don’t charge for the sea.” Then he asked Yves to tell him the story. Yves told it to him, sitting on a pile of nets, for an hour, eating sea urchins.

In the evening, Isabelle wanted to go to the Vieux-Port. She was looking for one particular café, the one where Odile had asked a young sailor for a light one day in June 1971. Yves found it without hesitating. The café had changed its name three times since, and the terrace was now covered with red parasols. But the corner table, by the street lamp, was still there.

They sat down at that table. The waiter, a young man in a hurry, asked what they wanted. Isabelle ordered a pastis for Yves, a coffee for herself and two grenadine syrups for the children. Then, when the waiter came back with the tray, she asked him, with a strange smile: “Excuse me, would you have a light?”

The waiter looked at her, surprised. “You smoke, madame?” Isabelle laughed. “No. Never. Neither did my mother, actually. She was just looking for an excuse to talk to someone.” The waiter didn’t understand. Yves did. He took an old copper lighter out of his pocket, which Henri had given him in 1985, and lit it in front of her without saying a word.

The little flame trembled in the evening wind. Rose-Hélène looked at it, fascinated. Then she blew on it as hard as she could, like a birthday candle. The flame went out. Everyone laughed. Henri-Ion, who never wanted to be outdone, blew in turn, at nothing, very seriously, looking at the harbour.

On the way to the hotel, Julien received a message. It was Inès. She had been invited to speak on the radio the following Tuesday, on a big morning programme. She was asking whether she was allowed to tell the story of the sea. Julien showed the message to Isabelle. Isabelle read it, then answered herself, on Julien’s phone: “Yes. Of course. Leave the door open.”

That evening, before falling asleep, Rose-Hélène asked her father whether Odile was in the sea now. Julien thought for a long time. Then he answered that she was in the sea, yes, and under the lime tree at La Duchère, and in the waltz, and also a little in the silence. “Then she’s everywhere,” Rose-Hélène concluded. “So she hasn’t left.” And she fell asleep, very pleased with her reasoning.
Quel est le sujet du concours d’éloquence ?
Qui siffle les trois premières notes à l’Odéon ?
Que demande Isabelle au serveur du Vieux-Port ?
Fill in with the right connector (the hint is in brackets).
In addition, the project costs little.
That’s why I’m asking you to come.
On the one hand it’s expensive, on the other hand it’s useful.
The final version of Inès’s speech for the regional final. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud like an orator. Mentally underline every connector. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Ladies and gentlemen, this silence is expensive. Indeed, it nearly cost twelve orchestras. Today I am asked whether culture is a luxury. I would like to answer you in three steps.
First, one thing must be acknowledged. Admittedly, culture costs money. A violin, a hall, a teacher, all of that has a price. I don’t deny it, and I’m not naive.

However, a luxury is something you can do without. Now, in my neighbourhood, before the orchestra, one child in three didn’t believe they could do anything other than what their parents did. Today, it’s only one in ten.

Next, culture doesn’t only benefit those who play. Not only have the children learnt music, but their parents have also come back to school, to listen to them. Besides, my mother, who works nights, hasn’t missed a single concert.
Moreover, people often forget that culture connects generations. An old lady of eighty taught a little girl of three to whistle a waltz. As for me, I play the clarinet of a man I never knew.
Finally, and that is why I am here, culture gives a voice to those who had none. Consequently, it is not a luxury. It is a door. And I simply ask you to leave it open.
En combien de temps Inès organise-t-elle sa réponse ?
quelque chose dont on peut se passer
Consequently, it is not a luxury. It is a door.

Write (at least 250 words) in French an argumentative essay on the topic: “Faut-il rendre la musique obligatoire à l’école ?” Structure: introduction with the problem, 2–3 arguments, a counter-argument, conclusion. Use at least 8 different connectors.
I set out the problem in the introduction and announced the plan (d’abord… ensuite… enfin).
I added arguments with de plus / en outre / par ailleurs / d’ailleurs.
I used “certes… mais” for a counter-argument.
I used “en effet” to justify (not “en fait”!).
I ended with “par conséquent” or “c’est pourquoi” and a proposal.
Should music be made compulsory at school? The question divides parents and teachers alike. First, I will show its advantages; then I will examine the objections; finally, I will propose a solution.
Music develops concentration. Indeed, learning an instrument takes hours of attention. In addition, it teaches you to listen to others.
Admittedly, the curriculum is already very full, and some pupils don’t like music. Now, people don’t always like mathematics either, and nobody suggests abolishing it.
Moreover, for many children, school is the only place where they can touch an instrument. Besides, school orchestras have brought absenteeism down.
Consequently, I think music should be compulsory until the age of fifteen. However, every pupil should be able to choose their instrument.
Read the dialogue aloud, taking turns as Inès and Mrs Vasseur.
Read Inès’s speech aloud, pausing briefly after each connector.
Link 5 pairs of simple sentences aloud with “or”, “en effet”, “toutefois”, “en revanche”, “par conséquent”.
Give a 2-minute speech on “Le sport est-il un luxe ?”, with the structure d’abord… ensuite… enfin and at least one “certes… mais”.
